newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China troop move will stamp its HK rule at once.
newsitem.headline: China troop move will stamp its HK rule at once.

text.p: China will quickly stamp its rule on Hong Kong with a show of force -- 4,000 People's Liberation Army troops crossing the border on ships, helicopters and armour just hours after the British handover on July 1.

Future leader Tung Chee-hwa's office announced late on Friday that the troops, spearheaded by armoured cars, would arrive at dawn. The timing ensures that they will sweep in as the city slumbers following all-night handover parties.
Hong Kong's stock market had just closed at a record high on the last trading day of British rule, underlining a wave of public optimism for a prosperous future under China.

Outgoing Governor Chris Patten condemned the move as "a most appalling signal to send to the people of Hong Kong", who are still chilled by images of armoured personnel carriers and green-uniformed troops used in the massacre of unarmed students around Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
Britain's Foreign Office said it may send a "negative signal" to the world.

Although Beijing will be responsible for Hong Kong's defence, and was expected at least to match Britain's 10,000-strong force, few had expected it to risk inflaming local sensitivities so rapidly with such a blunt military statement.

"We don't need so many, and we don't need them coming in such a fashion, by air, land and sea," said legislator Emily Lau, an outspoken critic of Beijing. "I don't think it's necessary, but they like to act the bully."

Troops will enter shortly after the popularly-elected legislature is dissolved, and while U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, British Prime Minister Tony Blair and a host of foreign leaders are still in town.
Chinese naval vessels will churn through waters crossed a few hours earlier by the British royal yacht Britannia carrying Patten and heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles on their way home.
China trumpeted the decision on its evening nationwide television news, saying the soldiers would enter through three border posts, depicted in detail on a topographical chart.
Washington took the announcement in its stride, saying China was acting within its rights.

"They've always said they were going to put Chinese troops where the British troops were. That's not anything unusual. It's their territory," said a White House official, who declined to be identified.
One Western military attache in Hong Kong said: "The political fuss is overplayed."
"It's just the political game of the departing colonial power with wounded pride versus the triumphalist Chinese, rubbing their hands with glee and restoring their own pride and sovereignty."
Earlier on Friday, kilted soldiers of the Black Watch bade farewell to 156 years of colonial rule over Hong Kong with a skirl of bagpipes.

But their lament was drowned out by the ring of cash registers as stock investors piled into Beijing-backed "red chip" and other companies and drove the Hang Seng index to an all-time closing record 15,196.79.

Until now, China had been at pains to ease public concerns over the People's Liberation Army, ensuring that the 196 advance troops now in place spoke the local Cantonese dialect, and were even proficient at singing karaoke.

A total of 509 troops will arrive shortly before the handover ceremony at midnight (1600 GMT) on June 30. The next wave of 4,000 will be accompanied by 10 ships, six helicopters, 21 armoured cars and 400 other vehicles.
"I do think that it is most unfortunate that this decision has been made. We will continue to make representation and hope that this decision is reversed," Patten said.
"It doesn't sound to me the right sort of signal to send to the international community, and above all I think it is a most appalling signal to send to the people of Hong Kong."
As strings of flags of China and the new Hong Kong -- bearing the emblem of the bauhinia flower -- were strung along roads, dignitaries began arriving for an end-of-empire party.
Among them was former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher, who signed the 1984 agreement that hands Hong Kong back to China.

Signs of political unease bubbled beneath the surface, focused on the doomed outgoing legislature, to be replaced by a Beijing-picked chamber. Pro-democracy actists such as Lau and Martin Lee will be dumped.
"There is apprehension now as to the possible, and even very likely, loss of some of our freedoms," Lee told Cable News Network (CNN).
